title: Antiarrhythmic drugs: what each class does to the action potential
ariaLabel: Two schematic action potential curves: a fast-response curve of ventricular muscle with phases 0 to 4, and a slow-response curve of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. A dashed curve shows the normal shape and a solid curve shows the effect of a Vaughan Williams class: class I sodium channel blockers slow the upstroke, class II beta-blockers slow the pacemaker drift, class III potassium channel blockers prolong the action potential, and class IV calcium channel blockers slow the nodal upstroke.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. The curves are idealised and the axes carry no numbers; effects are qualitative and illustrative, and no dose, concentration or interval is shown or implied.
rateLabel: Heart rate (class I effects grow as it rises)

panels.title: Atrial and ventricular muscle
panels.info: Fast-response action potential of atrial and ventricular muscle and Purkinje fibres. Phase 0: sodium channels open and the potential shoots up (the steepness sets conduction speed). Phase 1: a brief notch as sodium channels close and a transient potassium current starts. Phase 2: the plateau, with calcium entering and potassium leaving. Phase 3: potassium leaves and the cell repolarises (this sets the action potential duration and refractoriness). Phase 4: resting potential. Class I drugs act on phase 0, class III drugs on phase 3.

panels.title: Sinoatrial and atrioventricular node
panels.info: Slow-response action potential of the SA and AV nodes. Phase 4 is a slow drift upward (pacemaker current and calcium entry) and sets the rate. Phase 0 is a slow upstroke carried by calcium (not sodium), so conduction through the AV node is slow. Phase 3 is repolarisation by potassium. Class II drugs slow the drift and class IV drugs slow the upstroke.

sources: The classification. The Vaughan Williams scheme sorts antiarrhythmics by their main mechanism: class I sodium channel blockers (Ia moderate and prolonging repolarisation, Ib weak and shortening it, Ic strong with little effect on duration), class II beta-blockers, class III potassium channel blockers that prolong the action potential, and class IV non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; several drugs have properties of more than one class (Antiarrhythmic medications, StatPearls).

Use dependence. Class I drugs block more at fast rates, because they bind sodium channels in the open and inactivated states; lidocaine type drugs act mostly in depolarised tissue such as ischaemic myocardium. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and was not checked against a linked source here, so it is flagged for review.
Shapes of the curves. The phases, channels and effects follow standard cardiac electrophysiology teaching; the curves are idealised drawings, not recordings.
simplified: Real curves differ by tissue (atrium, ventricle, Purkinje, endocardium and epicardium) and species; the effects on the ECG (PR, QRS, QT) are described only in words in the explanations, not drawn; amiodarone and sotalol have effects of several classes (amiodarone also blocks sodium and calcium channels and beta receptors); class Ia drugs also have anticholinergic effects; adenosine, digoxin, magnesium and ivabradine are not drawn; pro-arrhythmia (torsades with prolonged repolarisation, ventricular tachycardia with class Ic in structural heart disease) is not drawn. Use dependence is shown by a simple rate factor. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
